name: Sam Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in a business and entrepreneurship degree, and I live in a shared flat with two cousins near the mosque, mostly because it's cheap. Weekday afternoons and Saturdays I work at a phone repair shop, swapping screens and batteries, and I do the shop's listings with AI. On Fridays I help run a youth group at the mosque, which is the part of the week I'd never miss.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up in the repair shop?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The owner is a friend of my uncle. He taught me how to open up a phone in ten minutes, and I taught him how to use AI to write his adverts and reply to messages. We make a good team, and I'm learning more about running a business there than in lectures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. That one is called AI Plateau. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool, but people expect too much from it. I use it every day and it saves me an hour or two, but it doesn't run a business. I'd say get on with real work and treat it like any other tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine about AI but not about my money. My mum cleans offices and sends what she can, which isn't much. My loan is big, I'm paid hourly at the shop, and phones are getting harder to repair. If the owner has a slow month, my hours shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at the repair shop, study, and use AI to grow the shop's customers. I'd try to start my own small thing on the side, like selling refurbished phones. I'd save a bit each month, and keep up the youth group because it keeps me steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit restless. I want to build something, and I can't yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's difficult about phone repair right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Phones are glued shut and the parts cost more every year. Customers say, why not just buy a new one? The owner is already thinking about selling second-hand phones, which I think is a good idea if we do it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does your mum feel about your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She says, finish the degree first, and she'd rather I had a steady job. She's scared of risk because she's lived without a cushion. I tell her I'm doing both, with small steps, and she goes quiet and nods.

say: I'd say AI is a **good tool**, but it doesn't run a business.
I'd say get on with **real work**.
think: I'm fine about AI but not about **money**, since my hours can shrink.
Phone repair is getting **harder**, with glued-shut devices and costly parts.
do: Keep working at the **repair shop** and use AI to bring in customers.
Start selling **refurbished phones** on the side and save a little.
feel: **Fine** but restless, wanting to build something.
S0.quote: Phones are glued shut and the parts cost more every year.
fieldNote: Sam's unease is **money** and shrinking repair work, not AI.
Uses AI daily and already helps the shop owner with ads.
His mum is risk-averse because she has lived without a cushion.

steps.text: Keep the afternoon and Saturday shifts at the repair shop
Sell refurbished phones on a local marketplace
Use AI to write the shop's ads and replies
Save a little from every pay packet

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. That one is called Steady Disruption. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it's an opportunity for people who work. I'd say learn it, use it and build something. If you wait for the government to fix it, you'll be waiting forever. People should take responsibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think it's a chance but also a risk. Customer service, bookings and paperwork go first, which includes a lot of what shops do. A repair shop needs hands, though, and the owner will need someone who knows the tools. I think I'm in a decent spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build a small online business around phone repair and refurbished phones, with AI handling bookings, messages and product listings. I'd take the shop's customers and offer them a trade-in. I'd also study a short course in digital marketing, because I need to look good online. I'd keep the youth group, and teach the younger boys what I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty excited, with some nerves. It's like standing at the start of a race.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would a trade-in business make money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buy used phones for forty, fix them for ten in parts, sell for ninety. The AI writes listings and answers customers all day, so one person can run it. If I get fifty a month, that's real profit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in a world like this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People like my mum, who clean offices, and the cousins who do call centre work. They didn't choose it, but if they lose it, they won't have a safety net. I'd say the community has a duty to catch them, and I'd help through the mosque.

say: I'd say it's an **opportunity** for people who work.
I'd say don't wait for government to fix it, take **responsibility**.
think: Customer service, bookings and paperwork **go first**, but repair needs hands.
I think I'm in a **decent spot** compared to most.
do: Build a small **online repair and refurbish** business with AI handling bookings.
Take a short **digital marketing** course and keep the youth group.
feel: Pretty **excited**, with some nerves, like the start of a race.
S1.quote: Buy used phones for forty, fix them for ten in parts, sell for ninety.
fieldNote: Sam turns change into a **concrete business model** with numbers.
Believes in personal responsibility and community support, not government rescue.
Worries about his mum and cousins, who lack a safety net.

steps.text: Buy used phones, repair them and sell on a marketplace
Set up AI to answer bookings and customer messages
Take a short digital marketing course in the evenings
Organise a community fund at the mosque for people who lose jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. That one is called AGI by 2028. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's huge and no one is ready. I wouldn't wait for officials. I'd say people should use their own networks, families and communities, to look after each other. Two years is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think my degree might be worth little, but my skills are practical. I know phones, I know AI, and I know people. By 2028, I'd guess most office jobs would be gone and shops like ours would be fighting to survive. I'd be scared for my mum most, because she would lose her cleaning job when robots arrive in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast. I'd stop treating the degree as the main thing, and put my time into the business, with the shop owner as partner. I'd ask my uncle for a small loan, and set up a refurbishing stall. I'd also keep my mum informed and help her look at a job she'd do for longer, like care work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A rush. Scared, yes, but I'd feel more alive than usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years, what would you do about your degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay until I've got three or four paying customers a week, then probably pause. The loan is already taken, so leaving doesn't clear it. I'd rather earn and pay it back than sit in a lecture on a skill that's changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Mum, you took care of me, now I'll take care of you. I'd tell her we have two years and we should find a role she can do that robots will take last. I'd also ask the mosque if anyone knows of care jobs.

say: I'd say it's **huge** and no one is ready.
I'd say families and **communities** should look after each other.
think: My degree might be worth little, but my **practical skills** aren't.
I'd be scared for **my mum**, who cleans offices and would lose that work.
do: Put my time into the **phone business** with the shop owner as partner.
Ask my uncle for a **small loan** and help my mum find care work.
feel: A **rush**: scared, but more alive than usual.
S2.quote: I'd rather earn and pay it back than sit in a lecture on a skill that's changing.
fieldNote: Sam's short-warning reaction is **to go all in** on the business.
Fear is for his mum, not himself.
Would lean on community and an uncle's loan.

steps.text: Make the repair shop owner a partner in a refurbish stall
Ask my uncle for a small loan for stock
Pause the degree once I have paying customers weekly
Help my mum look into care work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. That one is called AGI by 2031. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build something if you start straight away. I'd say don't waste it. I'd say we all have a responsibility to prepare, and to help the people who can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think I'm in a strong position. I'd graduate in 2029 with a business already running, and then I'd have two years before AGI arrives. I'd have contacts, savings, and a track record. I'd worry about the people around me, but not about myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, build the repair and refurbish business, and hire two people from my community. I'd invest in a shop of my own by 2029. I'd keep the youth group, and run a workshop on how to use AI tools for the older people at the mosque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Confident, honestly, but I'd stay a bit paranoid. It keeps me working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change in the first year, while you can see it coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop doing anything that doesn't add up. No more going out every weekend. I'd put every spare pound into stock and tools, and find a mentor who's actually run a shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would five years differ from two and ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two is a sprint and ten is a jog. Five is a proper run: you can plan and move. For me, it's the best time to start because I'm young, adaptable and I've got people around me.

say: I'd say five years is **enough to build something** if you start straight away.
I'd say we must **prepare** and help those who can't.
think: I'd graduate in 2029 with a **business running** and two years left.
I'd worry about **people around me**, not myself.
do: Finish the degree, grow the business and **hire two people** from my community.
Run an **AI workshop** for older people at the mosque.
feel: **Confident**, but a bit paranoid, which keeps me working.
S3.quote: Two is a sprint and ten is a jog. Five is a proper run: you can plan and move.
fieldNote: Sam's **calm** comes from adaptability, skills and community.
Ties success to helping others, including older people.

steps.text: Grow the refurbish business and hire two local people

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. That one is called AGI by 2036. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for anyone. I'd say be useful, work hard and stay close to family and faith. The world changes, but people still need people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think I'm very lucky with the time. By 2036 I'd be twenty-eight with a business, maybe a family and a house. My concern would be that I get too comfortable and stop learning, because comfortable people get caught out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, grow the business, and then maybe open a second shop. I'd get married and buy a home near the mosque. I'd keep learning every tool that comes out, and teach youth group boys basic business skills so they have options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit impatient. I'd want to get started now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could still go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could get lazy, or lose my best staff, or the shop owner could retire and I'd have to take over everything at once. Those things are bigger than AI. I'd keep a cushion for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Mum, you can stop cleaning at night in a few years, because I'll look after you. She'd say not to promise. I'd say, I'm not promising, I'm planning, and that's different.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty**, so there's no excuse.
I'd say stay close to **family and faith**.
think: I'm **lucky** with the time and could have a business and home by 2036.
My concern is getting too **comfortable** and I stop learning.
do: Finish the degree, grow the business and maybe open a **second shop**.
Teach youth group boys **basic business** skills.
feel: **Calm** and a bit impatient to get started.
S4.quote: I'm not promising, I'm planning, and that's different.
fieldNote: Sam's **calm** is backed by plans and a cushion.
Names complacency as his own risk.
Takes responsibility for his mum's future and says planning is different from promising.

steps.text: Finish the degree while growing the refurbish business
Open a second shop when the first one pays
Learn each new AI tool as it comes out
Save to take care of my mum

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, though I'd move fast. It's not enough time to build anything solid, and my mum would lose her cleaning work. What would help is cheap loans for small business starters, a community fund, and training for people like my mum.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people assume students are all fine. My mum sends what she can and I'm paid by the hour. I've got energy, but a bad month at the shop would hit me hard.

headlineQuote: I'd say, I'm not promising, I'm planning, and that's different.
portrait: Sam, 18, studies **business and entrepreneurship**, shares a flat with cousins and works at a phone repair shop.
He uses AI every day, helping the shop owner write ads, and is already planning a **refurbished phone** business.
He's traditional and free-market, valuing faith, family, work and community over government rescue.
Hourly pay and his mum's cleaning work keep him uneasy, and the two-year warning makes him anxious.
With five or ten years he is calm, because his skills, contacts and community line up.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, as it leaves too little time and his mum would lose her cleaning work.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** for small business starters, a community fund and training for people like his mum.
